Wrongdoing means an action or behavior that is morally wrong, unethical, illegal, or a violation of accepted rules and standards.

It is exactly what it sounds like: the act of doing something wrong — something that harms others, breaks rules, betrays trust, or goes against what society (or the law, or ethics) considers acceptable.

The "wrong" in wrongdoing can come from different sources:

1. Legal wrongdoing — something that breaks the law.
A politician taking bribes, a company dumping toxic waste illegally, a person committing fraud. These are wrongdoings because they are crimes.

2. Moral/ethical wrongdoing — something that isn't necessarily illegal but is still deeply wrong.
A doctor secretly sharing a patient's private medical information with outsiders (if not legally penalized in a particular context), a manager lying to their team to cover up their own failures, someone betraying a close friend's trust for personal gain. These may not always result in arrest, but they are still wrongdoings because they violate honesty, trust, and fairness.

3. Professional wrongdoing — violating the rules or duties of one's job or role.
A judge favoring one party unfairly, a journalist deliberately fabricating quotes, an accountant manipulating financial records. These are wrongdoings because they abuse a position of responsibility.

The key point: wrongdoing covers all three of these. It is a broad word. Something can be wrongdoing even if it isn't a crime — as long as it is widely recognized as unethical or harmful.

Anyone — and anything — that has responsibilities or is expected to follow rules:

  • A person: "He was accused of wrongdoing after stealing from the fund."
  • A company or organization: "The investigation revealed corporate wrongdoing."
  • A government or institution: "Citizens demanded accountability for the government's wrongdoing."

Wrongdoing is not limited to individuals. Entire organizations can engage in wrongdoing — think of a pharmaceutical company hiding dangerous side effects from the public, or a bank systematically deceiving its customers.

Wrongdoing usually implies that the person knew (or should have known) that what they were doing was wrong. It carries a sense of deliberate or reckless bad behavior — not a simple innocent mistake.

If you accidentally trip and knock something over, that's not wrongdoing. But if you knowingly lie on a legal document, cheat on an exam, abuse your authority, or defraud people — those are wrongdoings, because there is a clear element of choice involved.

That said, "wrongdoing" doesn't always require malicious intent. Negligence — where someone is carelessly irresponsible in a way that causes serious harm — can also count as wrongdoing. A surgeon who operates while impaired, for example, is committing wrongdoing even if they didn't intend to hurt the patient.

Wrongdoing can refer to acts that vary enormously in seriousness:

  • On one end: a minor act of dishonesty, like an employee regularly taking small office supplies home for personal use.
  • On the other end: massive, systemic wrongdoing, like a government orchestrating the persecution of an entire group of people.

The word itself doesn't specify the degree of severity. Context tells you how serious the wrongdoing is.

Wrongdoing is most often used as an uncountable noun — meaning you usually don't add an "s" to it, and you don't say "a wrongdoing."

✅ "There is no evidence of wrongdoing."
✅ "She denied any wrongdoing."
✅ "The report exposed widespread wrongdoing."
✅ "He was found guilty of wrongdoing."

Less commonly, it can be used as a countable noun when referring to specific individual acts:
✅ "The committee listed several wrongdoings in their report."

But the uncountable form is far more natural and common.

• "The whistleblower came forward to expose the company's wrongdoing."

(She revealed that the company was doing something illegal or unethical.)

  • "He resigned, but maintained he had committed no wrongdoing."

(He insisted he hadn't done anything wrong or illegal.)

  • "Victims of the bank's wrongdoing filed a class-action lawsuit."

(The bank had acted dishonestly or illegally, harming many people.)

  • "Turning a blind eye to wrongdoing makes you complicit in it."

(If you see something wrong happening and deliberately ignore it, you share some of the moral responsibility.)
How Wrongdoing Differs from Similar Words

Understanding neighboring words will sharpen your grasp of this one:

Crime — wrongdoing that is specifically illegal. Every crime is wrongdoing, but not every wrongdoing is a crime. Lying to your best friend is wrongdoing, but it's not a crime.

Misconduct — wrongdoing in a professional or official context. A police officer planting evidence is misconduct (and wrongdoing). The word "misconduct" tends to stay within institutions; "wrongdoing" is broader and works in any context.

Misdeed — a slightly old-fashioned, often literary word for a specific bad act. "He atoned for his misdeeds." Similar to wrongdoing but less formal and more poetic in feel.

Sin — wrongdoing framed through a religious or spiritual lens. Sin implies a violation of divine law or moral law as understood within a faith tradition. Wrongdoing is more secular and general.

Transgression — crossing a moral or legal boundary; a formal, somewhat literary term. Very similar to wrongdoing, but often carries a tone of crossing a line that was clearly drawn.

Wrongdoing sits at the center — it is serious, formal, broad, and doesn't require a religious framework or a specific professional setting.

• Wrongdoer (noun) — the person who commits wrongdoing. "The wrongdoer was brought to justice."
  • Wrongful (adjective) — describes an action that constitutes wrongdoing or that is unjust. "Wrongful dismissal" (being fired unfairly). "Wrongful conviction" (being found guilty of something you didn't do).

Think of wrongdoing as an umbrella word that covers any action — by a person, a group, or an institution — that violates moral, ethical, legal, or professional standards in a way that is harmful, unfair, or dishonest. It is most at home in serious contexts: journalism, law, investigations, formal reports, and ethical discussions. When someone says "there was wrongdoing," they are signaling that something went seriously wrong — not a small slip, but a real breach of what is right.
